analysis.one_liner: Nearly doubles the pass-through tax deduction, extends it to high-income professionals, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make the pass-through business tax deduction permanent and nearly double it, from 20% to 43% of business profits, so the top tax rate on that income falls to 21%. It would remove every current limit on the deduction, opening it to high earners in service professions like law and consulting who are excluded today. It would also let owners restructure corporations without paying tax on any built-in gains, and it would repeal the federal estate tax entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of profitable pass-through businesses — partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships — would pay sharply less tax, and the biggest dollar gains would go to the highest earners because the bill removes both the wage-based limit and the exclusion for doctors, lawyers, and other service professionals. Heirs to very large estates would pay nothing after the estate tax repeal. Owners converting a corporation to a different structure would avoid tax on built-in gains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-earning business owners and large-estate heirs

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the qualified business income deduction permanent and raises it to 43% of profits (47% after 2025), which the bill's own terms say is designed to put business income at a 21% top rate — the corporate rate — rather than the top personal rate of 37%.

It repeals the limit that ties the deduction to wages paid, which today restricts the deduction for businesses with thin payrolls, and it deletes the exclusion for specified service businesses, extending the full deduction to doctors, lawyers, consultants, and financial professionals.
It redefines 'qualified trade or business' as any business except being an employee, so wage earners get nothing from the expanded deduction while business owners do.

It declares that changing a corporation's legal structure is not a taxable event when the owners, ownership shares, and assets stay the same, letting owners sidestep tax on built-in gains during a conversion.
It repeals the estate tax for deaths after 2022, which applies only to the largest estates; in 2023 the tax reached estates above roughly $12.9 million per person.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, in lost revenue — every dollar of the expanded deductions and the estate tax repeal must be made up through borrowing, other tax increases, or later cuts to federal programs. Wage earners get none of the expanded business deduction but share the revenue cost as taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and future program funding

drawbacks.text: The expanded deduction and estate tax repeal reduce federal revenue substantially, and the bill contains no offsetting tax increase or spending cut, so the cost lands on the deficit.

The benefits are skewed to the top: removing the wage-based limit and the service-profession exclusion directs the largest gains to high-income owners of law firms, medical practices, hedge funds, and real estate partnerships, while employees receive nothing under the bill's redefinition of qualified business.
Repealing the estate tax removes a tax that falls only on estates above the exemption threshold, so its benefits concentrate among heirs of the wealthiest few percent of families.

Making corporate restructuring tax-free when ownership is unchanged would let owners convert appreciated businesses without ever recognizing the gain, a tax-planning avenue available only to business owners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Genuine small businesses would pay less tax, but the bill's structure concentrates the money at the top: the largest beneficiaries are high-income professionals and large-estate heirs, the estate tax repeal and deduction expansion have no revenue offset, and the tax-free corporate conversion rule invites planning strategies. An honest supporter would concede the revenue cost is large and the distribution tilts heavily toward wealthy households.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ) introduced the bill on January 9, 2023.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and that is the last action of any kind in the record — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
Not a single member of the House signed on as a cosponsor over the two-year Congress.
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because the bill never moved: current tax law, including the 20% pass-through deduction and the estate tax, simply stayed in place. The groups who would have gained most — high-income business owners and heirs of large estates — lost an opportunity rather than gaining a benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody gained; tax law stayed the same

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill sit for two years until it expired.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the record shows only one Republican sponsor; no bloc or party position can be measured.

industries.industry: High-income pass-through business owners (law firms, medical practices, hedge funds, real estate partnerships)
industries.note: The bill would roughly double their deduction to 43% of profits and remove the wage-based limit and service-business exclusion that currently cap their benefit, cutting their effective top rate to 21%. Their gain comes out of federal revenue, which everyone else eventually covers.

Full estate tax repeal applies only to estates above the exemption threshold (about $12.9 million per person in 2023), so the benefit concentrates in the wealthiest families and reduces federal revenue for everyone else.

industries.industry: Owners of profitable small and mid-sized pass-through businesses
industries.note: Ordinary profitable small businesses would keep the deduction permanently and pay less tax, which is the bill's advertised purpose; but their share of the benefit is smaller than the share flowing to high earners, and the revenue loss affects all taxpayers.
Tax-free conversion of corporate form would spare owners tax on built-in gains, a planning benefit available only to business owners.
